questions.prompt: A colleague says an open-weight model is 'the same as open source.' What's the most accurate reply?
options: Agreed — both mean the model is free to use
Open-weight means the model file is downloadable; training data and code are not necessarily public
Open-weight means the training data is public but the weights are encrypted
They are the same except open-weight is the marketing term
questions.explanation: Open-weight only requires the weights to be public. Training data, training code, and the recipe used to build the model may all stay private. Conflating the two is a common mistake.

questions.prompt: You need to summarise a confidential internal report. The report cannot leave the building. Which kind of model do you use?
options: Frontier, because it gives the best answers
Open-weight, because the prompt stays on your machine
questions.explanation: A frontier model sends the prompt to a remote datacenter. The constraint 'cannot leave the building' rules that out. An open-weight model running locally is the only option that satisfies the constraint.

questions.prompt: Which of these is the actual defining difference between open-weight and frontier models?
options: Whether the model is open source
questions.explanation: The reframe: the difference is whether the weights are public. Size and quality are correlated but not definitional. A large, high-quality open-weight model is still open-weight; a smaller, hosted model is still frontier.

questions.prompt: You want to fine-tune a model on your own support tickets. Which kind of model do you need?
options: Frontier, because it has the most parameters
Open-weight, because fine-tuning needs access to the weights
Either — fine-tuning is API-based for both
questions.explanation: Fine-tuning means continuing training on your own data. That requires editable weights. Frontier models ship weights you cannot download, so you cannot fine-tune them. Only open-weight models allow it.
